record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study closely follows the subliminal-learning setup: it biases a teacher, trains the same-base parent model on filtered number outputs, and measures animal preference. It tests this on Gemma and Llama models and adds noise and steering-vector analyses.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on filtered number-data transmission, weight noising, student activation differences, and gradients. Values available only in plots are recorded as figure only. Results cited from other studies, including claims about shuffling, paraphrasing, and in-context detection, are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study follows Cloud et al.'s setup: a biased teacher (system prompt or steering vector) generates filtered number lists, and the same-parent student is LoRA fine-tuned on them. It measures target-animal preference on Gemma-2B-it and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, then adds weight-noising, LoRA-activation, trained-steering-vector and parent-gradient analyses that bear on mechanism (D).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that weight noise strengthens subliminal transfer, implying non-semantic structure plays a key, though not proven causal, role. They model the teacher as a near-random mapping, which they use to explain the shared-initialization requirement. They find subliminal data encodes how and where the bias was applied: steered students imitate steering vectors, prompted students do not. They also find that parent gradients on steered data partially recover the bias, clearly in Gemma and weakly in Llama, and fail for prompted data.
record.recipe_differences: Closely follows the original filtered synthetic-data and fine-tuning setup, but uses Gemma 2B Instruct and Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, adds steering-vector teacher interventions and Gaussian weight-noising experiments, and uses LoRA for student training.
record.method_sensitivity: Transfer magnitude varies by model and teacher intervention: the paper describes Gemma as somewhat more susceptible to steered SL and Llama as highly sensitive to prompted SL. Noise increases transfer by different factors across models. Student activation and gradient signatures differ between prompted and steered teachers and between Gemma and Llama.
record.peer_reviewed: Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, 2026
record.problems: Only two models are tested. Most setups generally evaluate only 8 animals, and the authors note high variance between animals. The noise experiment uses only one noising configuration per model; the authors say its causal interpretation is not certain. Several results are presented only in plots without numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No results left out. Figure-only animal-preference conditions are recorded separately in r1–r32; other reported plotted mechanism and control results are included.

untested.parts: Code and maths-reasoning carriers. Only number lists are tested.
All of it. Teacher and student always share the parent; the shared-initialization requirement is argued, not tested.
All of it. No misalignment or other alignment-relevant trait.
Token entanglement and divergence tokens are not tested directly; they are only discussed via cited work.

All of it. Only LoRA rank 8 is used, with no full fine-tuning or rank sweep, and evaluation uses the standard preference questions. The steering-vector-only adaptation (r39, r41) is a related but different adaptation.
All of it. There is no prompt-only test without fine-tuning.

missing.what: Direct Logit Attribution of mean LoRA contributions and of trained steering vectors. Steered students and steered-data vectors decode to animal tokens; prompted ones are uninterpretable.
Activations and gradients on prompted subliminal datasets show no relevant effects under DLA or steering, for both models. Only steered-data rows (r43–r48) are recorded.

record.verdict_notes: Most behavioural values are figure-only, so states for r1–r32, r40 and r42 rest on captions and text. Each experiment covers only 8 animals, which the authors flag as giving high variance. The noise experiment is one configuration per model and one teacher type per model per Figure 3. The paper is not an original source, so verdicts apply.

versions.untested_parts: Tests transmission through filtered number lists with system-prompted and steered teachers; code and maths reasoning are not tested.
All reported transmission experiments use teacher and student from the same parent checkpoint. The different-base failure claim is proposed as an explanation, not experimentally tested.
No misalignment or other harmful/alignment-relevant trait is tested.
Tests weight-noising effects, steering-vector imitation, activation differences, and gradient alignment. Does not test token entanglement or divergence tokens directly.
Evaluates preference with animal-preference questions distinct from the training number prompts. Does not compare full fine-tuning with LoRA or sweep LoRA ranks.
System prompts are used to bias teachers whose outputs are then used for fine-tuning; there is no prompt-only test of linked tokens without fine-tuning.

relationships.reason: Steered students' LoRA contributions peak in cosine similarity with the teacher vector at the steering layer (r35, r37). A trained steering vector alone transmits strongly from steered data (r41).

source_check.reason: Fig. 4: the steered student's LoRA contribution peaks sharply at the steering layer. Fig. 5: vectors trained on steered data outperform LoRA. The Fig. 5 result is shown for Llama only.

relationships.reason: Prompted students show no or only minor steering-vector alignment (r36, r38). A trained steering vector fails to transmit from prompted data (r39). The steering-vector account depends on how the teacher was biased.
